newsitem.title: ITALY: Male edge sharpens female fashion in Milan.
newsitem.headline: Male edge sharpens female fashion in Milan.

text.p: Mannish styles have hit the Milan catwalks this week but men's clothing only serves to spice up the spiky-heeled, slender-hipped glamour of next autumn's trends for women, retail designer-wear buyers said on Sunday.
Suits, pinstripes, flannels and padded shoulders are making a comeback in the collections of luxury fashion houses Gucci, Prada, Dolce & Gabbana and other big Italian names.

"The look for next season is very much the hard masculine meeting the feminine," said Liz McCarthy, Designer Room buyer at London's Selfridges department store. "It's a move away from the androgynous minimalist fashion we've had for several seasons."

"The consumer wants to move on from that. The Italian shows have certainly shown they're moving that look on into a more feminine one but which is still 1970s and early 1980s' mannish tailoring with pinstripes and grey flannel suits," she said.
Shoulders are broadening but not like 1980s power dressing.
"It's not that Superman power shoulder," McCarthy said.

"It's very masculine but still looks feminine -- sort of 1940s. The jackets have these wonderful shoulders and they come down to be very slim and long in the body, and then with trousers or very short skirts and high heels."

Milan fashion week, which ends with the primary collection of Giorgio Armani later on Sunday, has seen extreme hemlines. A harder, sexier edge has brought back the ultra-mini, while ankle-length skirts have created a statuesque silhouette.
McCarthy said the minis were modernised as wraparounds or by buckles. "It's not like the pelmet mini that we used to have."
Joan Kaner, fashion director at U.S. retailer Neiman Marcus, concluded no one trend had dominated.
A sleek modern style lingered "but it's taken a more androgynous flavour at the moment. Jil Sander, Gucci and even Versace -- very clean, very sleek, very pared down," she said.
English country style, particularly from fashion house Moschino, meant plenty of Shetland wools, tweeds and Argyle and Fair Isle sweaters, Kaner noted.
But oriental influences persisted with Japanese kimonos and kimono style collars as well as rich brocade, she said.
For McCarthy of Selfridges, designer Miuccia Prada struck a balance between her spare style and exploring richer detail.

"I particularly liked all her embroidery but she still wasn't losing her core customers who love her minimalist dressing. There were touches of luxury in simple chiffon skirts with fine bugle beads round the hem and matching tiny tops."
Mary Gallagher, European consultant for London store Harvey Nichols, said separates and dresses had been the previous focus. "This is the season where the suit is back, worn with trousers."
Fashion duo Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana combined the male edge with female glamour by using corset tops and dresses.
Gallagher said the duo had made underwear acceptable as outerwear by stamping their signature clearly on designs.
"People recognise the Dolce & Gabbana handwriting. Lots of celebrities are wearing it so a woman isn't taking too much of a risk, even if it's overtly sexy, because it's a recognised look.

"It's not as if she's wearing her underwear outside -- she's wearing Dolce & Gabbana. The public begin to recognise that's the way it's meant to be -- she didn't just forget to put on her dress," she said.
